It wasn't until the end of the dinner, where my partner mentioned that he was taking me on a client dinner on behalf of a large investment bank, where Nick finally acknowledged our presence in front of his eyes.  For the first time during the night, Nick awoke and asked my partner about typical 'allowances for client dinners' and 'which investment bank had the highest dinner and lunch allowance'.  'How is Morgan Stanley ranked relative to Goldman Sachs?', he asked.  Very shallow.

Truly a low-brow experience.  Strongly recommend you avoid this restaurant.

Must have walked past the place 3 times until I saw the number on the door. It's one of those "almost" hidden places.

Walking in the vibe is great! Where else do you hear drake & Jay Z while eating omakase? The staff was extremely personable & that beautiful wood counter made the space so visibly pleasing.

We went with the sushi omakase being we weren't extremely hungry. When the first piece was toro I knew this place was going to make me a very happy girl! All pieces were delicious, only thing I may possibly change is the size of the pieces. Tended to be on the smaller side. Then again, there's 20 coming your way and I'd have to say I was full after dinner, 3 additional pieces, & dessert.

The standout piece for me was the seared toro (had a different name) wrapped in nori. Lordddddddddddd was that amazing. I could eat a whole 20 piece meal based on that alone. Dreaming of it now actually....

Oh, apple pie was bomb. My boyfriend kept making fun of me when I said we get apple pie here! And asked the waitress if this amazing Apple pie exists to try to test me. BOOYA, I do my research. 

Add shuko to your sushi list people! You won't be disappointed! And will most certainly be back.

A fantastic meal. The first dishes take creative dishes, lots of fun combinations that properly know how tastes support and combine with each other. All killer, no filler during this portion. If you've been to Soto, this is along similar lines but more interesting. During the second half of the courses, things move to the sushi and our chef was brilliant. He was personable with his bar (two couples total) and modified his sushi as we dug into the pieces. I'm still debating between this and Sushi Nakazawa for this particular portion of the dinner, it's a difficult choice. Shuko serves enough food to make you feel like exploding. At the end, we were slowly waddling out of the restaurant towards Union Square.
Had the kaiseki here a few weeks after they opened. What a wonderful time. Great food.

The food is great but I'd say the atmosphere and interaction are severely lacking compared to restaurants in the same price bracket (emp, ichimura, etc). It seemed like chefs Kim and Lau were so inconvenienced with having a successful restaurant. They hardly interacted with their patrons even though this place was 20 or so (cramped) seats. 

The place felt like it was too small for both the patrons and the chefs. They were constantly running each other. If you want to spend this much for an intimate omakase / kaiseki I'd go elsewhere. 

To be fair the food and drinks were great.  The fish was incredibly fresh and seasoned perfectly. Even the rice was flavored expertly and was the right texture and temperature. I'm sad I missed out on the squab Pete wells raved about but tonight we had a veal cheek instead. Veal cheeks were perfectly tender and had great balance. 

I'm not sure if I would be back based on the lack of interaction with my chefs. I can say though that although chefs Kim and Lau were too busy a lower level chef did a great job talking to me and my companion and kept us entertained. He was the saving grace service wise.

There is always something new occurring at Shuko. Chef Nick is great. After his team's venture at Neta, Shuko really shows his clients what he wants to create with his food. (right down to the 4-5 inch hand-sanded wood counter.) The service is great and the occasional hot dishes from the small kitchen in the back are unique and cooked to perfection.

I recommend dining here is if you are looking for more of an out-of-the-box japanese/sushi meal because it is not traditional and reflects the chefs' experimentation and creative power. Apple pie at the end of the meal as well as the homemade brioche for the fatty tuna + caviar are super cool.

For the price point, I expected to be wowed.  Unfortunately, the food isn't at the wow level.  I enjoyed the atmosphere and music plenty.  Service was good, not the best.  Basically it all comes down to the food for me though.  We opted for the kaiseki ($175) plus the ($50) wagyu supplement.  Many of the kaiseki plates were on the bland side.  Our wagyu plate was over salted and slightly overcooked.  The sushi portion of the meal was good, not great.  There was a guy preparing 10 sushi pieces at once and doing it quickly.  That doesn't happen in a top Japanese sushi restaurant.  I liked some of the finishing dessert courses.  

The best part of the meal was being able to bring my own bottle of Champagne for $30.  We ordered an expensive bottle of sake off the list so the house waived our corkage.

In summary, for a high tariff I want to be wowed.  Too many of the dishes were just average and not seasoned correctly.  Nice to try but no return visit for me.

the dinner was ok until this nick kim guy just went on an ego trip. after the kaiseki course, i was feeling just one more maki to finish it off. i asked the assistant chef if they had tamago or kanpyo or torotaku which i usually order when i go to other sushi places such as 15 east or jewel bako - they did not have any of those. out of nowhere nick kim comes at me asking if i was japanese...do i know the season for fish of this specific salmon...(i didnt even ask for salmon?) with the wrong tone and attitude. basically he was saying why do you ask for kanpyo etc if your not japanese. i still dont understand what the deal was with this guy. maybe he was having a  bad day but this guy was just angry that we asked for something they didnt have and that is no way to treat your customer. anyone would expect tamago from a sushi place. this place is a eat what we serve you, we're from masa minded. overly arrogant for the non-memorable food + $900 dollar price tag. way overpriced for what they serve. i feel like NETA is way better than this place. (kaiseki menu is very similar to neta's) and i understand why neta let go of nick kim. he has some personality issues..i feel bad for chef jimmy he seems like a nice guy. this place maybe ok to try once...but i will bet you will not come here twice.

My husband and I had our anniversary dinner there and it was the best omakase ever in NYC! We ate at Masa, too but we felt Shuko is much more satisfying than Masa in many ways..phenomenal savory dishes and sushi courses, friendly setting, amazing chef, Jimmy, great crew etc etc. Thanks Shuko for the wonderful dinner, our life felt so much fuller after your meal.

After reading the bad reviews I'm pleased to say that I'm glad I didn't read before going. I can only imagine that with all businesses there will always be mistakes made which in the end opens opportunity for a business to recover and correct their mistakes. We came in past hot food being served but was happy to have the host to give us a couple of seats at the end of the bar and enjoy omikasa. As visitors to New York we tend to be more enthusiastic about our food explorations.  Our dinner on a Sunday night was the highlight of our visit. Interior design and service was impeccable and the attention to detail was exceptional. The sushi & sashimi was fresh and a delicious curation of complimenting each serving. I would highly recommend this restaurant even if with bad reviews, I write a review because although there may be some dissatisfied customers, whatever the case may be, we thoroughly enjoyed our meal and would highly recommend.  Despite all previous negative comments, we enjoyed our visit because most issues have resolved. Service, food and interior details was amazing.

Shuko does a very good job. I dined alone and they made it very comfortable, not the easiest thing to do, trust me. The toro, toro sinew and tempura maitake mushroom really stood out on the kaiseki menu. I wasn't as impressed with the lobster and the tuna with caviar and milk bread as expected. Overall a very good experience. Negotiate the wine pairings, they will give you very good pours. I got $70 worth and some. Good value. The sushi dishes come quickly. Apple pie at the end I thought was a cocky slap in the face but also a cop out. Service was on point, food is worth it. I would return. Spent $350 total, tax and tip included. Kaiseki, wine pairing and extra toro sinew course cause I'm a fatass. Go. I'm a Wall Street guy but I hate hanging around novice ass Wall Street skeletons who don't know shit about food and spend their time sharing Tinder strange with the guy next to them. Bro you are 50, stop looking for 21 year old strange that is only impressed by Kors purses and Burch flats.
The food at Shuko is incredible. Great, intimate ambience and always playing cool hip hop in the background. Stellar service (that you'll be paying for).

shuko.  i wanted to love you.  i wanted to say that every damn reviewer out there had it right.  i really just liked you, but we're still friends rah?  

dude if ima drop 500 hundo plus on a dinner u better be mind blowing.  the biggest knockout that was given was santa barbara uni.. not to sound like a snob but been there done that, doesn't differentiate from the other places out there.. some pieces were standout but when you're serving toro it's hard not to be good.. it's the other stuff that irked me.  the warm plated dishes just didn't deliver to me.  i loved the decor, the service, have always been a fan of jimmy and nick but for the price point i just don't get it..

As close as it can get to a true five-star restaurant. I am quite sure they will reap one or two michelin stars in the next edition of the guide. 

We sat at the counter and enjoyed a well orchestrated succession of well-prepared dishes, in a japanese yet very friendly setting. While the bill can be quite steep, this is a great place to experience with your +1 on a special occasion.
This may be the best fish in NYC (with the exception of Masa), Each piece was sensational.  The chef crafted each bite.  The sushi is the reason to go.  Go for that.  Enjoy it.

Having eaten at Neta, I think the  chefs at Shuko were being held back.  Shuko is sublime. We had cocktails and the Kaiseki menu. The attentiveness of  staff was fantastic: aware, but not overbearing, never did we feel rushed, and the interaction between the staff was excellent, efficient.  Our sushi chef very memorable, and his attention to detail, and our personalized tastes, was as part of the experience as the taste. The only drawback, if it can be called such, was that the dessert was more tepid, and twice the size it ought to be.  Otherwise, perfection.

Not the best sushi I've ever had, but very very good.

We did the kaiseki, and I would definitely recommend that over the sushi omakase.

While the sushi was great, I thought Shuko's strengths were the dishes that were unique.  For example, I loved the grilled toro sinew - it was absolutely delicious.  The maitake on crispy rice was also incredible and super creative in that the texture of the maitake mimicked a fish tartare.

The apple pie with bay leaf ice cream at the end was excellent - perfect end to the meal

the food and setting are five stars.  the fish is spectacular and our sushi chef was a master (andrew from indonesia).  interesting, inventive combinations of flavors, textures.  numerous oohs, and ahs.  lovely, comfortable setting.

what grates is the service.  asked 'still or sparkling?', my husband and i hesitated for a moment, and were told, 'you can have sparking and still'.  it felt like an offer, and we accepted (many high-end restaurants provide filtered and carbonated water, at $135 per person, it wasn't a stretch to imagine they would here).  when i saw they opened two bottles of hildon, i thought, 'great, that'll be $10 each' - and it was; this does not add to the experience.  i'm not a militant environmentalist, but shipping glass bottles across the ocean is sillyness.  and it's not that we can't afford it or are stingy, it's about expectations.  worse was the fact that they 'topped up' aggressively.  so much so, we noticed.  we were not asked if we would like another bottle, or to finish the other half full bottle - another bottle was opened (and left 3/4 full).  indeed another $10.  

our 'waitress' had attitude, which we could just bear, but things got worse with the appearance of an 'overlord': a bearded hipster we overheard snapping: 'she finished her saki, ask if she wants more'.  he was constantly pressuring the waiters to serve and sell more drinks, add ons.  unashamedly, and within earshot.  with wine it was the same - constant top up . . . and it worked.  we polished off the bottle and so ordered two more glasses of the same (excellent) wine.  two glasses were more than 50% of the cost of the entire bottle.

if we had just ordered tap water and had realized that they were actively trying to up the bill by upselling, we would have resisted and left much happier.  there are too many other excellent omakase restaurants where you won't feel squeezed.

the crowd they attract is kind of annoying as well - one woman was just thrilled to show off how much money she could spend, which was off-putting, and an overly eager banker regaled his embarrassed client with puffery and gross exaggeration.  luckily there were a number of gracious and dignified guests as well, but the overall tone isn't as peaceful or congenial as it could be (i suspect the 'overlord's overbearing demeanor is infectious).

though we loved the food, i doubt we'll rush back.

We'd heard many good things about Shuko, but getting reservations here is hard - the only reservation consistently available right now is at 5:30 PM, which is a tough time to swing except on the weekend. We got lucky and snagged that time this past Saturday and finally got visit one of the city's newest - and one of its best - contributions to the phenomenal Japanese food scene here. The entrance is an innocuous wooden door, which reminds me of the subtle entrances to contemporaries such as Soto and Neta. However, the decor is a seamless blend of Japanese influence (smooth wooden cabinetry, wooden countertop) with New York edge (exposed brick walls), and the music is reflective of this fusion - I'm pretty sure you've never heard 'Big Pimpin' playing in the background at any other high-end Japanese restaurant. The more casual atmosphere is great as well; no one was super dressed-up; I wouldn't say it's a shorts/t-shirt place in the summer, but you definitely don't have to be done up fancy to eat here. All the servers here are accessible and chatty, and we even got to talk a little bit with Jimmy Lau as he was cutting the sushi part of the course - you don't get a terrorist fist jab from most chefs at these kinds of spots!

Although the chefs come from Neta, I felt the food here was superior and more interesting across the board, even when it's clear where the inspiration for some dishes came. The toro with caviar and milkbread is as good as ever, but the Osetra caviar adds a much more distinct salty contrast to the rich fattiness of the toro. Just as good (and possibly better) is the wild trout with trout roe and tempura flakes; the richness of a good cut of trout is hard to beat in terms of depth of flavor, while trout roe has a bit more of a concentrated flavor relative to ikura, making for a spectacular bite. The roasted lobster was so good - lobster by itself is great, but toss in some succulent bacon bits, cauliflower that's been cooked with truffles (and truffle oil), and you have a dynamite dish that you wish you could have more of, given the melange of rich flavors in a light dish. The meat dishes were fantastic as well, with the braised oxtail cooked perfectly, and the wagyu ribeye being mind-blowing. It's not cheap ($50 supplement for 3.5 ounces), but it is by far the best cut of beef I've had in a long time - such richness of flavor, succulence abound, and paired with mushrooms to give a bit of earthy balance. Don't even hesitate when asked about it if you are having the omakase...it's practically a requirement to try it.

We eventually made it the sushi portion of the meal; the sushi was delicious overall, although a couple pieces (namely the fluke and the lean tuna) were noticeably less fresh than the other pieces we had. However, most of it was delicious, with a wandering focus onto less-visited fishes (like baby sea bream, which was so good, and a very textured - yet still creamy - piece of sweet shrimp that is my favorite version of this piece so far. The toro was first - and was fantastic - and the skipjack was perfectly done as well. Some of the pieces come with light garnishings akin to Sushi of Gari, but it's less intrusive / less of a showcase than it is there. One piece I particularly liked was a piece of 'sushi' that was really marinated mushrooms served on crispy rice - I loved the crunchy texture, which reminded me of slightly overcooked mochi. In all, you get around 12-14 individual pieces, as well as a couple of rolls (the negitoro does not fail to impress). When you're done polishing off the sushi, you get a cleansing tangerine sorbet, and then apple pie! It may be a bit jarring relative to the rest of the meal (which, outside of the steak, is pretty light), but it's so good - great caramelizing of the apples, and the highlight is the bay leaf ice cream; it's such a subtle flavor that doesn't hit until the back of the mouth, but it is incredibly good - I'd eat it on its own.

With a very solid drinks menu - I had a cocktail and a craft red ale from Japan, and you can do a drinks pairing if you're so inclined that spans all different kinds of booze - this really is the complete meal experience. It will set you back for sure - the kaiseki is $175 (the omakase is $135) before the wagyu supplement - but it was one of the most enjoyable and complete dining experiences I've ever had in NYC. Highly deserving of all the praise and unquestionably deserving of the Michelin star(s) that it hopefully will earn later this year, and one of the few high-end restaurants where you walk out feeling like you got a fantastic experience all around and you really got the bang for every buck.

Tuesday night dinner for 2 @ 8pm. 

We got the kaiseki ($175/pp) and a bottle of sake. The kaiseki includes mochi appetizer, a salmon dish, dungeness cucumber salad, tuna and caviar on milk toast, lobster-bacon-mushroom-cauliflower dish, scallop and vegetable tempura, squab with purple carrots and a clear mushroom soup to cleanse the palette before the sushi course. Standouts were the tuna topped caviar and squab. The dishes came out super fast. As soon as we were done with our last bite the next dish was in front of us. 

Chef Nick Kim is the man! He is so friendly and personable. He really made our experience at Shuko. When we were served the sushi course, he was very quick and efficient assembling the sushi while conversing with us. The sushi pieces come with less rice than your normal omakase sushi pieces, probably half the amount. So on top of our kaiseki, we requested 4 additional uni pieces each - Santa Barbara, Maine (x2) and Hokkiado. All were fresh and delicious! I'm a fatty so I didn't think I would get full but by the end of the meal, I was nursing a good buzz and a food baby.

A fun, tasty, and pleasant experience. 

The staff and chefs were warm, friendly, and welcoming. We opted for the full tasting menu and it does not disappoint. Everything was expertly prepared and delicious. Lovely textures and flavors and the sushi quality was pretty up there. Although the cuts of fish were a bit on the smaller side. The uni was a generous portion though.

The staff was attentive and quick without being clumsy or overbearing. The wood countertop is unique and a beautiful piece of white ash. A lot of attention to detail in both the decor and food.

Overall, a great experience and I dont even feel bad about spending over $500 for a dinner for two.

The sushi omakase was top notch and definitely competes with some of the top sushi places in NYC that have at least  one Michelin star or not (Yasuda). Some of my favorites included the buttery, soft oh toro and the Hokkaido uni. Yuzu was a prevalent  theme throughout many of the courses.

I partook in the $135 sushi omakase - a couple of hours of wolfishly tonging plate after plate of perfect, pink, glistening sea-morsels that straddled the visual divide between "foodporn" and "NSFW". It was the thoughtful little additions to each nigiri that made Shuko real standout sushi -- an unexpected droplet of ponzu or yozu or truffle oil or pink salt on top that gorgeously complimented the fish, like, oh, I don't know, a yellow accent table or snazzy drapes do a room. 

The omakase was in all probably about twelve to fourteen pieces of fish - and not all created equal, to my mind. My "complaint" is therefore that there's set menu only (omakase or the $170 kaiseki) -- the velvet ropes of restaurants -- a move that at once elevates Shuko far above a spur-of-the-moment meal, and also forces you to take the bathwater (the clam; the tuna maki, for two) down with the, uh, baby. 

Sushi counter only (be mesmerized), or try and score the private room downstairs for group.

I'm so sad to have to write about how disappointed we were with our experience at Shuko.  I was super excited to try it, since I adore sushi and love Neta. We'd initially had a reservation for three, but as soon as we found out we'd only be two, we adjusted our reservation immediately, out of courtesy to the restaurant.  We emphasized at that point, and again left a message the day before our reservation to confirm, that we'd be seated at the sushi bar.  When we got there, we were shown to a small two-seat table instead.  We asked why we weren't being seated at the sushi bar as requested, and were told that because were now a party of two, we couldn't sit there, but they'd try to move us to the bar when someone got up.  Of course that never happened, and we watched as four seats at the sushi bar were unoccupied for the first hour of our meal.  
This wasn't the most auspicious start, but we nonetheless settled in for a great meal.  I am allergic to wasabi and told the waiter as much.  He then brought over a little side of wasabi for my friend, saying that since I wasn't eating wasabi, it was easier for the chef to just make both our meals without wasabi.  This struck us as really strange.  Just because I can't eat wasabi doesn't mean my friend shouldnt be able to enjoy her meal the way it was meant to be!  Each piece is made individually, after all.  Well, our first pieces of sushi came out.  The chef seemed confused about which pieces had wasabi, but thought he had it figured out (one side had a ton so it was easy to see).  I ate my first piece of sushi, and lo and behold, got a big mouthful of wasabi.  All six pieces were loaded with it. When we called the waiter over, he took the plate away and instead of giving us new pieces of that course, moved on to the next, sticking the first course back in later only when we reminded him.  All of the sushi was pretty good, although I noticed that it felt like half of our pieces of sushi were tuna - we had three different lean tuna preparations alone.  There was no seafood, clams, etc.,  that all of the reviews had spoken so highly of; the most 'exotic' fish was a scallop.  When we reached the last course, I asked why there was no uni since I noticed that the table next to us (there are only two tables in the place, the rest of the seats are at the bar) had had it as part of their standard sushi tasting menu.  The waiter told us if we wanted uni we'd have to pay extra!  We asked him to check in again, and were brought over some uni by Nick Kim, who apologized for 'messing up all night' by continuing to give me wasabi - by bringing over pieces of uni covered in - you guessed it - wasabi.  It would have been like a comedy of errors if not for the fact that they'd made me sick by serving me something I couldn't eat without really seeming to care.  What if my allergy had been a really serious one instead of just giving me a stomach ache?  I've eaten sushi at lots of great places, including Neta, and have never had an issue before, much less such continuing issues, with this request.  If a restaurant serves someone with allergies their allergen after a specific request, I'd expect a lot more contrition rather than just a shrugging off.
We spoke to the manager at the end of the meal, and the main thing that he and the waiter had to say was that we should come back again and it 'would be better next time.'  Given the price of the meal, I don't know why I would possibly want to pay that much money n a meal again when my first experience went like this. I guess I'll never get to try those interesting clam and seafood preparations. The service was completely indifferent and we were definitely treated like we didn't matter as much as the other customers - first with our seats, then with the care given to our dietary instruction, then with the types of sushi served to us.  Maybe if we'd been finance bros or distinguished older men (i.e. someone guaranteed to leave a great tip) we'd have been treated a lot better?  That's certainly how it seemed.  It sucks to have been looking forward to a special occasion meal so much, one that was a real splurge for us, and have it be so different than all of the great reviews, and such a letdown.

I've recent rediscovered Shuko.  The scallops are as good now as they were the first time I had them. The service is friendly but slow, which isn't a bad thing.  And I love the crowd.  It's the day before St Pattys day and Shuko has a dignified demeanor that beckoned me in and keeps me coming back.

I would not recommend this restaurant to anyone. I went there last night and was treated very rudely simply on the way I was dressed. I asked for a seat and it was obvious that manager looked me up and down and judged a book by it's cover. Dressed for the cold weather, I was not wearing the "appropriate" attire. And although there were 4 seats at the bar, she stated that "there was no room".  And actually followed me to the front door to make sure I left. I have never been treated so poorly at any restaurant.  I only visit New York for business and always find a Sushi Bar downtown.  I wish I could comment on the food. I will never try to eat at this bar again and would not recommend it to anyone based on the blatant disrespect of the manager.

I just had dinner at Shuko, and, unfortunately, was very disappointed. We chose the Kaiseki option (only the squab - from the cooked dishes - was really good; the others were okay). When I made the reservation, I requested Chef Nick. Big mistake. He and Chef Jimmy were there. The problem, however, was that while Chef Jimmy was busy cutting the fish he would later use to make sushi, Chef Nick was walking around, rearranging plates etc. One of the sous chefs (very nice and friendly) prepared our sushi. It was good, not great. When we left, Chef Jimmy smiled and thanked us for coming. For $500 I expected a lot more.

What a delight!  Shuko was a wonderful dining experience, spring for the kaiseki option, its a lot of food, but you get the best of both worlds with the kitchen dishes and sushi options.  Yes the seating is a bit twice and service can be spotty throughout the night, but the food is amazing.

Had dinner at Shuko last night.  We were originally seated at a table but the hostess kindly moved us to the bar at our request.  We were seated in front of chef nick kim.  Ordered two cocktails, one tequila and grapefruit based bad one sake based.  Both were just okay, but a nice way to start the meal.  Sake menu is overpriced, but expected.  We ordered the sushi omakase ($135 per person) which had about 20 pieces.  If you are a sushi purist (whatever that means), Shuko is not that.  However, I really enjoyed my meal.  This is much better than neta, the fish was fresh and enjoyed the pace of the meal.  Nick was engaging and was happy to make special rolls for customers per their request.  I love that they toast the seaweed before making a roll or sushi, just adds a little something.  Also, the restaurant is done well and love the large bar format.  Overall very good, pricey, different from nakazawa but in a pleasant way.

Having made a reservation for a Saturday night quite a few weeks ago, I was doubly excited to eat at Shuko after Pete Wells gave this place 3 starts in his review. Who wouldn't right? Well, I hate to be the bearer of bad news, but for me, the way this place is run and the experience that is ultimately given to the diner warrants a much lower score-- Shuko in its current state, is very undeserving of such high praise.

When we first walked in, the ambiance seemed just lovely--the decor was refined, elegant, but not stuffy, a physical manifestation of the tone that Nick and Danny wanted to reflect in their establishment. We were seated a table to the side of the sushi bar so visibility was great as well.

The problems started when, within 10 minutes of our being seated, three different servers came and asked us if we were ready to order. We had a few questions about the menu and each server basically gave us a different answer to the same questions... Firstly, don't these guys communicate with each other at all during service? And more importantly, given that this restaurant is the product of two Masa veterans, shouldn't the waitstaff have some sort of training about the menu itself? How on earth does management allow for their servers to run around from table to table with what seems like absolutely no knowledge of the food that they are serving?? 

This latter issue is my main gripe with this restaurant. We were having a hard time choosing between the omakse and kaiseki menu and asked one of the servers if he can ask if uni was part of the kaiseki? The server let us know that he wasn't "entirely sure" but would first check and then let us know if it was not. Since within 5 minutes of that conversation, the food that started arriving at our table  was part of the kaiseki menu, we assumed that uni was good to go, I mean, who wouldn't right?

Lo and behold, after some 10-12 courses, the meal had ended and no uni had been served...This might seem like a really paltry thing to gripe about, but the fact of the matter is that when you are dropping $500 on dinner for two, clear communication about what a person is to expect is a must. Had the server just come and to us and let us know that uni wasn't on the menu or it wasn't available, then our expectation for that particular item would not have been let down and that would have been the end of that story. 

But it wasn't. The worst part of all this was how management handled the situation. On the evening that we went, the floor manager/GM(?) seemed to much rather schmooze with her friends that were dining there than to bother checking up on other diners. We know this because her friends were sitting right next to us and she would periodically come over and talk to them, rather loudly and bumping into my partner, disrupting our meal completely. This was the last straw.

By the time dessert rolled around, we took a few quick bites out of courtesy and started looking around for someone to ask for the check. No one came to us and soon, our "looking around" became glares cemented onto our pissed-off faces. 20 minutes later, a check was handed to us and it was only as we were leaving, that the manager asked how our dinner was. Our response was terse but polite and her feigned concern about our disappoint was well noted.

In short, Shuko is a gleaming, beautiful ship, carrying wonderful treasure suffering from wood rot. What is the point of having good, if not potentially, great food if the management is a disaster and your service staff is laughably ignorant of the menu? For me, it's too soon for Shuko to be resting on its laurels, and I will not be returning.

Amazing restaurant, would definitely come back. We got the Sushi Kaiseki and it was the perfect pairing of warm dishes with a fresh selection of some of the best quality sushi I've had. I loved how their sushi emphasized the natural taste of the fish without adding much of anything else sauce/garnish-wise. The cooked dishes added nice variety to the meal so I would highly recommending getting this over just the sushi tasting.

Ambiance was quiet and relaxing, with everyone seated around the sushi bar. Great place for a nice refreshing meal to unwind the day.

Went last week.   Best sushi I've had in NYC - maybe ever.   Have not been to Nakazawa yet, but have been to most of the other highly acclaimed sushi places in the city.   Can't think of a better one.   Very simple and to the point - omakase and some wagyu.   That's the menu.  And it is about perfect.  Ambiance and service were great.  

If you can get a reservation and don't mind spending some money.    Go for it.    

PS - probably better for 3 people or less since it is sushi bar style sitting.

Omaske was simply divine. Although this wasn't a true omaske, Shuko gravitated to dishes we are familiar with at any Japanese  restaurant and took it one step beyond. The one dish that took really stood out for me was the Concord grape granita. The dish was refreshing and left a longing impression to go back again. 

Heck, I'll probably go back just to hear the music. Keep up that playlist...

KenScale: 8.5/10

Shuko is a new omakase tasting restaurant opened by chefs Nick Kim and Jimmy Lau, formerly of Neta. Unlike Neta, which I had visited previously, the dining area is a lot smaller and pretty much intended for a tasting menu on the counter where chefs can deliver each dish on a real time basis. While Neta was more oriented toward small plates that you can order a la carte, Shuko has a bit more ambitious proposition, with two different tasting menu options (sushi-only omakase at $135 per person and kaiseki style omakase with both sushi and non-sushi components at $175 per person).

I went for the sushi-only omakase option, and really liked many of the pieces that I sampled. Each piece had its own seasoning (i.e. no need to dip it into soy sauce) such as yuzu sauce, and the texture of the rice was just about right with optimal temperature. I loved the freshness of various fish pieces, from toro to fluke to Spanish mackerel to uni to tuna. The thing that most impressed me about Shuko perhaps is many unique pieces that you don't ordinarily see elsewhere. I savored the melting sensation of toro sinew, and a variety of mushroom pieces were quite outstanding as well. You can tell that Shuko isn't just settling with a pedestrian omakase menu. Each piece served on my table had its own flavor and texture that was telling its own story, and reflected the dedication of the chefs helming the counter. The sushi tasting menu will come in slightly over 20 pieces, so you'll definitely get staffed by the end of the meal.   

The restaurant has a variety of wine and sake menus, but my suggestion is to just order a bottle to go along with the tasting menus. Shuko has a trendy, modern vibe that at the same time doesn't strike you as an over-the-top, stuffy place. Getting a reservation could somewhat be a challenge so I suggest booking early. Yes, the price tag can be a bit intimidating, but if you're looking for a memorable omakase experience, you're in good hands at Shuko.
I haven't had better sushi in NYC.  Phenomenal.  Great service, great drinks, and the fish is outstanding.  The music and the vibe make this place one to which I will return many times.

Exceptional omakase, and I'm a picky eater! It's a small restaurant with most seats around a large kitchen/bar. You have your own itamae, slicing each fish and presenting it beautifully right in front of you.  

The sushi was unbelievable, my favorite being the toro which just melted as it touched the tongue. I was also impressed with the inventive mushroom dishes.

I loved the vibe, the setting, and the music. Everything was PERFECT and I can't wait to go back!

I had an excellent dinner this past Tuesday at Shuko. I went for the Sushi Kaiseki menu. The cost is $175. My favorite dish was the lobster/bacon/truffle/cauliflower dish. The dinner began with a mochi/miso/pistachio square. Followed by a crab salad and a bowl of toro/caviar that was excellent. This was followed by a dish of sea trout and trout eggs; vegetable tempura pancake style; and short rib that was very tender and flavorful. Before the sushi was served, there was a bowl of dashi with a Matsutaki mushroom. Chef Nick took excellent care of me (as did all of the staff). Wine and water glasses were refilled promptly. I had a lovely bottle of a 2012 Donhoff Spatlese that paired beautifully with everything. Looks like (from my photos) that I had 13 pieces of sushi and 2 hand rolls. When I was done with the sushi, Chef Nick asked me whether I was still hungry, and since I'm used to large tasting menus, I said I still had a bit more room for more food. A lovely bowl of spicy trout was brought out to me from the kitchen that was delicious! Two desserts: a lovely Concord grape granite and a large slice of apple pie with bay leaf ice cream. I think the apple pie slice could be a bit smaller. Seating was comfortable. I'm very happy I had dinner at Shuko!

Would be nice to keep it a secret .... but truth is, it doesn't get better than SHUKO!!! I was three pieces in on the sushi tasting and didn't want to take another bite because I didn't want it to end. EVERY single bite was magic. counting the hours until I go back... T-32. 

Nick, Jimmy, Jerrad --brilliant! was worth waiting for. the food, presentation, vibe, the MUSIC .. おめでとう

The three of us had their $175 tasting menu; it consists of 7 cooked dishes, 12 delicately individually prepared sushi and 2 desserts.  It's as good as any of the best we had in Tokyo.

The preparation is pure, material is exceptional and service can't be beaten!

This is a destination spot; don't miss it.

I've been twice and both meals were outstanding with the most recent visit last week being one of the best meals I've had in NYC in a while. Toro tartare and caviar and the grilled tuna sinew roll at the end were standouts. Krug Grande Cuvée (old disgourgement) was a perfect pair to almost everything

4 stars for the sushi bar ! For the kitchen 1 star. Sushi is as fresh as fish gets ...Textures...insane !! The slight touches of lime zest & shiokambu on sushi makes it perfect...doesn't overwhelm the freshness of the fish which sushi of gari fails miserably. The rice cooked to perfection & nori CRISP !! Combined with Santa Barbara uni melted in my mouth like a butter on hotcakes. The unique plates that looks like cracked bricks and walls was a great touch to originality. Indra who I'm so lucky to have as my sushi chef gave me a perfect second act with his grace, care & detail for perfection. The first act however was the reason I never went back to Neta. Ponzu, shiso, cilantro, cucumber, tempura flakes & bacon steals the show ruining my lobster, Dungeness crab & sea trout. Toro caviar was not a surprise, Masa took that part of me long gone. I prefer sliced toro over scraped toro nowadays, seen too much with scraped toro to have any affection. Music is a bit too jumpy for me from rap to jazz to Pop, rather prefer elegant instruments with my sushi. Ambiance was simple & elegant. Nice touch was fist bumps all around to regulars. Behind the counter all the chefs were great ! Attentive ! Great attitude ! But other then that I don't know if you know what I mean. At $175 is it worth it ??? Mos Def !

I think it was over 2 years ago when I first tried, and fell in love with, Nick and Jimmy's unique and utterly spectacular dishes at Neta. So, to put it lightly, I had arguably the highest of expectations possible when I first dined at their new spot - Shuko - just two weeks ago. My expectations were not only met, but exceeded. And that is saying a lot.

The place has arguably one of the most sophisticated storefronts I've ever seen. Cooler than Neta's, something I can imagine as the front of a gorgeous but understated $10m townhouse in the West Village or something. The ambiance could not have impressed me more - casual, yet elegant. The music was as good as it gets, nicely curated - and the volume, the mood, were set just right. The decor was impressively modern. It's one of those unique places where I think it'd be just right bringing a date, your parents, or a business dinner - just like Neta was, but I think even more versatile.

Onto the food. I don't take pictures of my food, sorry - and it's been two weeks, so I can't remember every dish I had. However, I remember the overall experience. And it was spectacular, as good as Neta or Masa at their best. Of course they had the "classic" favorite you can get at Masa, Bar Masa, Neta - the Toro Tartare, which is impossible to not love. And I also remember the scallop, which is my quintessential favorite dish from Neta as well as here. I remember a couple great cooked dishes as well, things different from Neta, as well as some things the same. I'm not a big fan of dessert, so can't speak for that. And, of course, who can finish a review without writing about drinks. The drinks were awesome, and their new drink guy was as good as it gets! Just ask him to make you something special, and I'm sure he'll impress you - I was.

Honestly, I also can't speak much for value. I don't think experiences like Neta, Bar Masa, Masa, Shuko, Nobu, Ichimura, etc should be compared on that basis. It's all expensive, and it's all a once-in-a-while experience. It's just about whether it's worth it or not, to have some "special" occasion there. For me, talking about Shuko, it totally is. It's about as good as Japanese food gets in NYC.

One word....WOW!! From top notch chefs to unbelievable ambiance Shuko sets the bar. I love the locations discreteness, as well as the bar setup. The ability to interact with the chef really makes this a must try. The quality of ingredients really helps their creative dishes standout. Having tried all the NY staples, such as Masa, Sasabune, Nazakawa, Shuko takes the best of them all and combines them in one intimate and fun experience. I would highly recommend trying to lock down a reservation.

I was super excited on getting a reservation here only a week out and for a good time slot, 8pm. As others have said this is the new spot from the old chefs from Neta. I actually like the ambiance a lot better here, its a better place for a date. Food was very good and i was happy that they still had old favorites like toro tartare with caviar and the scallop with truffle and mushrooms along with a few new ones. Dessert was apple pie with a bay leaf ice cream which was really tasty and satisfying 

Im a huge fan of the cooked food start and the sushi end and thought the price of 175 was good for the level of ingredients we were given. Service was attentive and polite, I would definitely return

I have been to Shuko twice, once at the bar and once downstairs in the private room, both of my experiences were absolutely phenomenal. I have been to all the top places in the city for their omakase...from Masa, to Yasuda to Sushi of Gari, and this has been by far the best. From the level of exceptional service to the atmosphere, to the attention to detail in every dish, it all comes together to create an absoutely amazing experience. They have taken it to the next level with drinks, i tried this drink they call the Bob Dylan, and it was one of the best/most unique drinks I have ever had. All in all this is a very special place that i will be visting often with both clients and friends!

I had a great time at Shuko, we sat at the bar and had one of the best meals i have had in ages.  The service was great, very personal and made our experience extremely enjoyable.  I can't wait to go back for more.  I would highly recommend this restaurant to anyone looking for a great atmosphere while enjoying phenomenal dishes!

Being big fans of Jimmy and Nick at Neta we were very excited to try their new spot.  Unfortunately, it was a very disappointing experience.

Food:  We have tried every top Omakase in the city and this one at a pricey $175 pp woudn't make our second tier list.  Way too many mediocre hot dishes from the kitchen followed by an OK selection of sushi to follow.  Hot dishes all came with fancy ingredients (truffles, caviar etc) but were pretty flavorless for the most part with a few exceptions.  The hot menu at Neta was much better, although admittedly we stopped going after Nick and Jimmy jumped ship.  We were already full by the time what we  actually came for (the sushi) started.  We were then underwhelmed by the actual sushi and its preparation.  We were especially disappointed that they had a Su Chef prepare our sushi at the bar while Nick relaxed swigging wine and Jimmy prepared sushi for the tables.

Service:  They sat us down at 9:50 for our 9:00 PM reservation.  Normally I would have walked out after this kind of scheduling mess but we were too excited to try this place and cut them some slack since the place opened just 2 weeks ago.  Then we found out we likely got bumped because of celebrities that showed up last minute which did not sit well with us as full price loyal customers.  They did compensate us by comping our full alcohol bill of around $150.  Frankly, they seemed to be too distracted by the celebrities and friends in the place to properly service all the high paying clientele in the sushi bar.  This may be a good marketing strategy to hype up the place but will kill them in the long run when they need the regs to keep coming and shelling out $600 on a meal for 2.  At these numbers they should be making sure every detail is taken care of.  

Ambiance:  They play cool old school hip hop and attract a younger outgoing local crowd so it is a refreshing vibe compared to most plain and quiet omakase spots and the overly fancy tasting menu shrines from the celeb chef crowd.

In this hyper competitive space with soaring retail rents, hopefully they will get their act together before the hype subsides and the place crashes and burns.  They are very talented but this level of effort won't cut it.

"It's a world of difference between good and great."

I want to start with some numbers. $175. This is the cost of the kaiseki menu. You wouldn't know this if you walked in cold, because no one tells you in advance. In fact, there's no food menu at all, not even a tour guide sheet to help you suss out what you're having in case you happen to miss the server's spiel. Personally, I don't find this terribly expensive for what this experience could be--could--but it is worth keeping this number in mind as I continue.

Three. That's the number of sakes available by the glass. Imagine going to your favorite trattoria and finding only three by-the-glass-wines. You'd laugh, right? You'd assume, sure enough, there were a few other bottles available by the glass. Not at Shuko. Only three sakes, all of which are delicious but none of which particularly showcase some of their umami powerhouse dishes. No yamahai, really? No nama genshu? Who exactly is running this bar program?

6. That's when my reservation was because there was literally nothing else available, even several days before Shuko opened. Fine, I can live. But despite this, we were seated by the door (not even at an edge with extra room, I had to ask for that!) on a cold November night. Even my simple seating change request was met with uncertainty.

Worse still were the service levels. The staff were all (for the most part) nice, but coordination was sloppy and objection handling was abysmal. What do I mean by that? My fiancee, a petite woman, politely informed the chef that she was getting full partway through the meal. Unlike Nakazawa, where Nakazawa himself began using less rice for her so she could enjoy all the pieces, we simply got a shrug and a rattling off of items left to eat. Great. Thanks for the help.

I had my own embarrassments too. The sushi rice is so loose that it often crumbled in my hand when I tried to pick up my pieces, making me look like a messy clutz. And when I asked the chef to repeat the Japanese name of a fish he himself had told us, he couldn't do so. I even asked in Japanese (I'm conversational in the language, but don't look it), and he simply said: "No, fish not from Japan". Yes, thank you, I know. I simply wanted to hear the name again for my own benefit.

$175. Remember that number? Does this sound like the service you expect for that price point? How about a hostess who looks like a bored intern (so much so that I kept forgetting if she was a guest or staff)? How about a patron who comes in and starts putting their belongings in my fiancee's chair as we're getting ready to leave?

Food-wise, there were some hits (especially the kaiseki items) and a number of misses. Sequencing of the sushi was all over the place. First piece, blue fin. Second piece, shima aji. Really? Do you serve a steak dish before a white fish one? The pieces towards the end--the negi toro roll, for example--made for a lackluster finish.  The uni was a fishy disappointment.

If this were a $100 or even a $120 omakase, I could let it slide. But not at $175. Between the service, the inconsistency of items, and the lack of transparency online and in the restaurant, all I could think upon leaving was that it's going to take a hell of a lot for me to go back to Bar Shuko. This is one to pass on, at least for the foreseeable future. Head to one of the other many more polished experiences in NYC and you'll probably even save some cash.

I love this place!! The ambience, the service, and food are fantastic. We were amazed by the freshness of the ingredients and the details that the chef put on to every plate. I recommend this restaurant 1000%

Pricey. Service was solid and we thoroughly enjoyed the music selection. Good food but nothing wowed us. Appreciated the caviar, seared toro, scallop, and the squab. Pleasantly surprised by the grape kakigori and apple pie a la mode to finish the meal..
